(16.1) the two standard non-Noetherian examples: k[X_1,X_2,…] and the subring {a+Xg} of k[X,Y]
Exercise (16.2): every generating set of a finitely generated module contains a finite generating subset
Definition (16.3): the ascending chain condition (acc) and the maximal condition (maxc) for ideals
Lemma (16.4): acc holds if and only if maxc holds
Proposition (16.5): Noetherian, acc and maxc are equivalent for a ring
Example (16.6): the non-Noetherian ring k[X, X/Y, X/Y^2, …] inside k(X,Y)
Proposition (16.7): R/a and S^{-1}R are Noetherian when R is
Exercise (16.8): if R[X] is Noetherian then so is R
Exercise (16.9): a subring of a Noetherian ring admitting an R-linear retraction is Noetherian
Theorem (16.10) (Cohen): a ring is Noetherian if every prime ideal is finitely generated
Lemma (16.11): if R is Noetherian then R[X] is Noetherian
Theorem (16.12) (Hilbert Basis): a finitely generated algebra over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian
(16.13) Noetherian modules, the identification of the submodules of the regular module with the ideals, and the module form of (16.5)
Lemma (16.14): nested submodules with equal intersections with N and equal images in M/N are equal
Exercise (16.15): prove or refute (16.14) for two submodules that are not assumed nested
contents.reason: Altman–Kleiman poses this as a prove-or-refute exercise testing whether the nesting hypothesis of (16.14) may be dropped; the answer is a counterexample about two unrelated submodules of the middle term of a short exact sequence, which belongs to the general module chain-condition development rather than to Noetherian ring theory, and no proof on this pair uses the un-nested form.

contents.name: Proposition (16.16): M is finitely generated / Noetherian in terms of N and M/N
Corollary (16.17): a finite direct sum is Noetherian exactly when each summand is
Exercise (16.18): ⊕R/a_i is a Noetherian R-module, and R is Noetherian when ∩a_i = 0
Theorem (16.19): over a Noetherian ring, Noetherian, finitely generated and finitely presented agree for modules
Exercise (16.20): Hom(M,N) is finitely generated for finitely generated M and N over a Noetherian ring
Lemma (16.21) (Artin–Tate): the intermediate ring of an algebra-finite tower is algebra finite
Theorem (16.22) (Noether on Invariants): the invariants of a finite group of automorphisms are algebra finite
(16.23) the Artin–Tate proof of the Zariski Nullstellensatz
contents.reason: This derivation needs a transcendence basis of R over k and the field-theoretic Zariski lemma, neither of which this pair develops; the Nullstellensatz block is where that machinery is assembled and where the Artin–Tate route is one of the two proofs on offer.

contents.name: Exercise (16.24): algebra-finite field extensions of a Noetherian domain and of its fraction field
contents.reason: The exercise is the field-extension form of Artin–Tate that feeds Zariski's lemma; it presumes the fraction-field-versus-algebra-finite dichotomy that the Nullstellensatz page establishes, and stating it here would leave its only interesting direction unusable.

contents.name: Example (16.25): the ideal (2, 1+√−5) of Z[√−5] is finitely presented and locally free of rank one but not free
contents.reason: Localisation of modules at a prime and the local criterion for freeness are needed to state, let alone prove, this; both belong to the later commutative-algebra development, and the example is the standard first witness that an invertible ideal of a Dedekind domain need not be principal.

contents.name: Definition (16.26): Artinian modules and rings, the descending chain condition and the minimal condition
Proposition (16.27): Artinian versus minc, submodules and quotients, and finite direct sums
Exercise (16.28), Noetherian half: a finite-dimensional algebra over a field is Noetherian
Exercise (16.28), Artinian half: a finite-dimensional algebra over a field is Artinian
contents.reason: The Artinian half needs the descending chain condition and the length machinery that the Artinian-rings pair develops; proving only the Noetherian half here keeps this page's subject single and leaves the Artinian statement to the page that can also say what it is worth.

contents.name: Exercise (16.29): Z[1/p]/Z is an Artinian, non-Noetherian Z-module
Exercise (16.30): an Artinian domain is a field, so every prime of an Artinian ring is maximal
contents.reason: This is the opening move of the structure theory of Artinian rings and is only useful once the descending chain condition is available as a working hypothesis; it says nothing about Noetherian rings and belongs with the dimension-zero results.

sources.title: J. S. Milne, A Primer of Commutative Algebra, v4.03 (23 March 2020)

contents.name: Proposition 3.1: finite generation, the ascending chain condition and the maximal condition are equivalent for a ring
Remark after 3.1: a quotient A/a of a noetherian ring is noetherian
Proposition 3.2: the same three conditions for a module
Remark after 3.2: the submodules of A regarded as a module over itself are exactly the ideals of A
Proposition 3.3: nested-submodule equality, finite generation, and the noetherian condition across a short exact sequence
Proposition 3.4: every finitely generated module over a noetherian ring is noetherian
Proposition 3.5: a finitely generated module over a noetherian ring has a finite filtration with quotients A/p_i
contents.reason: The filtration is the first result about associated primes and its whole content is the primality of a maximal annihilator; it is the opening lemma of primary decomposition and is proved there with the associated-prime vocabulary that makes it usable.

contents.name: Aside 3.6: ideals maximal with respect to a property are frequently prime
Theorem 3.7 (Hilbert basis theorem): every finitely generated algebra over a noetherian ring is noetherian, proved through the leading-coefficient ideals a(i)
Corollary 3.8: over a noetherian ring every finitely generated algebra is finitely presented
Nakayama's Lemma 3.9
contents.reason: Nakayama's lemma is about an ideal contained in every maximal ideal acting on a finitely generated module; it needs the Jacobson radical and is the organising result of the localisation-and-support pair, where its corollaries on minimal generators live.

contents.name: Corollary 3.10: elements generate M exactly when their residues span M/mM over the residue field
contents.reason: This is the minimal-generator corollary of Nakayama and is meaningless without it; it is stated over a local ring and belongs beside the construction of the residue field and the support of a module.

contents.name: Corollary 3.11: the minimum number of generators of the maximal ideal equals dim m/m^2
contents.reason: This corollary defines the embedding dimension of a noetherian local ring, which is the invariant the regular-local-ring pair is built around; placing it here would leave the reader with an invariant and nothing to compare it to.

contents.name: Example 3.12: Nakayama fails for the non-finitely-generated Z_(p)-module Q
contents.reason: The example only makes sense as a hypothesis test for Nakayama's lemma, which this pair does not state; it also needs localisation of Z at a prime as a worked object rather than as a definition.

contents.name: Remark 3.13: the nilpotent-ideal version of Nakayama, valid without finite generation
contents.reason: This is a variant of Nakayama's lemma with the finite-generation hypothesis traded for nilpotence of the ideal; it is a refinement of a statement this pair does not carry, and separating it from the lemma it refines would leave neither legible.

contents.name: Definition 3.14: the height of a prime ideal and the Krull dimension of a ring
contents.reason: Height and Krull dimension are defined by chains of prime ideals and are only useful once the spectrum and the principal ideal theorem are available; the dimension pair is where the convention for the zero ring is also fixed.

contents.name: Lemma 3.15: every generating set of a finitely generated ideal contains a finite generating set
Theorem 3.16 (Krull intersection theorem)
contents.reason: Milne's proof runs through homogeneous polynomials in the generators of the ideal, which is the graded and Rees-algebra machinery; the Artin–Rees pair builds that machinery and derives the intersection theorem from it.

contents.name: Proposition 3.17: in a noetherian ring every ideal contains a power of its radical
contents.reason: The statement is about the radical of an ideal, which this pair never defines; the radical, the nilradical and the finiteness of the nilpotency exponent are introduced together on the prime-spectra page.

contents.name: Aside 3.18: no uniform bound on the number of generators; (X,Y)^n needs at least n+1
Aside 3.19: the Krull intersection theorem fails for the ring of germs of smooth functions at 0
contents.reason: The witness is the germ of exp(-1/x^2), and the counterexample needs germs of infinitely differentiable functions together with the fact that all of its derivatives vanish at the origin; that is smooth-function analysis, and it also refutes a theorem this pair does not state.

contents.name: Exercise 3.20: the subalgebra A = k + k[X,Y]X of k[X,Y] is not noetherian

contents.name: Theorem 8.1: a ring satisfies the ascending chain condition for ideals if and only if every ideal is finitely generated
Examples after 8.1 (1)–(2): fields are noetherian and artinian; Z and k[x] are noetherian and not artinian; every PID is noetherian
Example after 8.1 (3): k[x_1,x_2,…] is not noetherian, and its fraction field shows a subring of a noetherian ring need not be noetherian
Example after 8.1 (4): every artinian ring is noetherian (forward reference to Theorem 12.4)
contents.reason: Hopkins' theorem that an artinian ring is noetherian rests on the finite chain of powers of the Jacobson radical and on module length; both are the subject matter of the artinian pair, and the notes themselves defer it to their own §12.

contents.name: Lemma 8.2: any quotient ring of a noetherian ring is noetherian, and likewise for artinian rings
Theorem 8.3 (Hilbert's Basis Theorem), proved by the stagewise leading-coefficient ideals I_j and degree reduction
Corollary 8.4: any algebra of finite type over a noetherian ring is noetherian
Lemma 8.5: a localisation R[S^{-1}] of a noetherian ring is noetherian
Definition and example after 8.5: the ascending chain condition on submodules, and R is noetherian exactly when it satisfies it on R-submodules
Lemma 8.6: the middle term of a short exact sequence satisfies the ascending chain condition exactly when both ends do
Corollary 8.7: every submodule of a finitely generated module over a noetherian ring is finitely generated
Theorem 8.8: Spec R is a finite irredundant union of irreducible closed subsets, uniquely so
contents.reason: The statement is about closed subsets of the prime spectrum in the Zariski topology, so it needs the topology itself; the algebraic shadow of it, the finiteness of the minimal primes over an ideal, is where the radical is available.

contents.name: Corollary 8.9: in a noetherian ring the radical of an ideal is a finite intersection of prime ideals
contents.reason: This is the purely algebraic form of 8.8 and is stated in terms of the radical of an ideal and the minimal primes over it, neither of which this pair introduces; both are minted on the prime-spectra page.

contents.name: Lemma 8.10: in a noetherian ring (rad I)^N is contained in I for some N
contents.reason: The bound is stated for the radical of an ideal, a construction this pair does not carry; it also duplicates Milne's Proposition 3.17, and building it twice in two places would split one statement across two pages.

contents.name: Theorem 8.11: a finitely generated module over a noetherian ring has a finite filtration with quotients R/p_i
contents.reason: The proof turns on a maximal annihilator being prime, which is the definition of an associated prime; the filtration is the standard first theorem of that development and is unusable before the vocabulary exists.

contents.name: Definition after 8.11: a finite A-algebra versus an A-algebra of finite type, with k[x] separating them

contents.name: Proposition 5.1: equivalent conditions for a module to be Noetherian
Lemma 5.2: the Noetherian condition across a short exact sequence, with the nesting hypothesis made explicit
Proposition 5.3: a module over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian if and only if it is finitely generated
Lemma 5.4: for a module-finite extension of a Noetherian ring, every intermediate ring is module-finite and Noetherian
Theorem 5.5 (Hilbert basis theorem, first proof): the polynomial ring over a field is Noetherian, by induction on the number of variables through a monic reduction
contents.reason: This is a genuinely different second proof and would be welcome, but it turns on being able to assume that a chosen nonzero element of the ideal is monic in the last variable, which needs the Noether-normalisation change of variables; that lemma is scaffolded on the normalisation page, and rebuilding it here would mint a second id for it. Flagged to Alpha as an optional enrichment if the substitution lemma is pulled forward.

contents.name: Theorem 5.6 (Hilbert basis theorem, second proof): every finitely generated algebra over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian, by stagewise leading-coefficient ideals indexed by all of the natural numbers
Corollary 5.7: a ring finitely generated over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian
Theorem 5.8 (Emmy Noether): the invariants of a finite group acting by algebra automorphisms on a finitely generated algebra over a Noetherian ring are finitely generated
Remark after 5.8: a monic polynomial over a ring with zero divisors can have more roots than its degree
Corollary 5.9: a finitely generated algebra over a principal ideal domain is Noetherian
Proposition 5.10: a localisation of a Noetherian ring at any multiplicative system is Noetherian
§2.1 “Rings that are direct summands”, Proposition 5.11(a),(c): every ideal of a split subring is contracted, and a split subring of a Noetherian ring is Noetherian
Proposition 5.11(b),(d),(e),(f): surjectivity on spectra, the Artinian case, normality, and compatibility with localisation for a split inclusion
contents.reason: These four clauses of the same proposition speak about prime spectra, the descending chain condition, integrally closed domains and localisation of the splitting; each names a notion introduced on a later commutative-algebra page, and splitting the proposition across pages is preferable to importing four vocabularies in order to state one lemma whose Noetherian clause is all this pair uses.

contents.name: Example 5.12: the Veronese subring of a graded ring is a direct summand
contents.reason: The Veronese construction selects the graded pieces whose degree is a multiple of a fixed integer, so it needs a graded ring and its homogeneous decomposition; graded rings are built with the Rees algebra and Hilbert function machinery, and this is one of that page's standard illustrations.

contents.name: Example 5.13: the Reynolds operator retracts a ring onto its invariants when the group order is invertible
§2.2 “Noetherian induction”: the method of passing to a maximal counterexample quotient
Theorem 5.14: a Noetherian ring has only finitely many minimal primes, and so does every ideal of one
contents.reason: The statement quantifies over minimal prime ideals and its proof reduces to the reduced case by killing nilpotents; the nilradical, reducedness and the minimal primes over an ideal are introduced together on the prime-spectra page, which is also where the finiteness statement is first needed.

contents.name: Theorem 5.15 (Hilbert's Nullstellensatz, second strong form)
contents.reason: The Nullstellensatz relates radical ideals to vanishing sets over an algebraically closed field and rests on Zariski's lemma; both the vanishing-set vocabulary and that lemma belong to the normalisation and Nullstellensatz pair, and no Noetherian result on this page uses either.

contents.name: Proposition 5.16: in the spectrum of a Noetherian ring every closed set is a finite union of irreducible closed sets
contents.reason: This is a statement about closed subsets of the prime spectrum in the Zariski topology and so presupposes that topology; the Zariski page is anchored after the published topology pages precisely so that results of this shape can be stated honestly.

contents.name: Proposition 5.17: a subspace of a Noetherian topological space is Noetherian
contents.reason: A Noetherian topological space is defined by a chain condition on closed sets rather than on ideals, and it is introduced with the Zariski topology; importing it would mean defining a topology on a page that develops none.

contents.name: Theorem 5.18 and Remark 5.19: algebra homomorphisms into the base field as the points of an affine algebraic set, and inclusions of closed algebraic sets
contents.reason: These set up the dictionary between a finitely generated algebra and an affine algebraic set and then compare closed algebraic sets inside one another; that dictionary is assigned to algebraic geometry by the track's scope denials and rests on machinery this library has not reached.

contents.name: §5.1 “Formal power series rings”, Theorem 5.20: if R is Noetherian then the formal power series ring over R is Noetherian
contents.reason: The commutative-algebra design overlay assigns this to the present pair, but formal power series are constructed on the published page formal-power-series at plan order 193, far after this page's order of 111.001. Stating it here would need either a load-bearing citation to a later page in reading order or a second, silent construction of the power series ring, and both are barred. The remedy is to move a published page in reading order or to give the result a commutative-algebra home after that order, and both are owner decisions.
